answers.text: For example, I would tell the assistant: always reply with exactly three lines, in this order — delivery date, item and quantity, and any change from the original order. Anything else in the email gets ignored. That way it always comes out the same.
I would say: list each call with time, customer, topic, and outcome, always in that order. Add up how many need a follow-up call.
Something is not right with the price part, 100 units feels like a lot to confirm again over email like that. I would ask someone to check it before it goes out.
62 up from 54 works out to about 15%, so that part is fine. But 3 late out of 62 does not come to 97% — that is closer to 95% by my count.
I would go with the second one, it looks more careful and complete, with the numbers written out.
I would send the second reply — it has the order reference and the credit reference in it. The first one is nice wording but there is nothing you could check against.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. No, I would rather not paste it in without checking first. 5. No.
The pricing and discount numbers I would leave out, and the confidentiality clause too since it names both companies by name.
I would want someone to check the totals against warehouse numbers before it goes any further.

Step one worries me the most, because if the details are read wrong there, it carries through. But step four is also risky, since it sends automatically — I would want a person to look before that happens.
